title: Constant and changing increments
concept: A nonlinear response can change its increment as the input changes.
steps: Use inputs 2,3,4 for the quadratic rule and the separate one-unit linear pairs [2,3] and [7,8]. Keep the rules 10+2x and 10+2x+x squared distinct; they are constructed prediction rules, not causal estimates.
Calculate the squared column: 4, 9 and 16. Add the starting level and both contributions to obtain quadratic predictions 18, 25 and 34.
Subtract adjacent predictions. The quadratic increments are 7 and 9 for equal input steps; the linear increments remain 2.
Read the left graph as the two response shapes and the right graph as the three hand calculations. The transformed-column diagram shows that both x and its square enter the weighted sum.
slide_steps: Set x to 2, 3, 4; calculate the squared column.
Compute predictions 18, 25, 34 and increments 7, 9.
Compare with the constant linear increment of 2.
practice: Calculate both rules at x=5 and x=6; report their increments.

title: Turn a known condition into an indicator
concept: An indicator is one when its stated condition holds and zero otherwise.
steps: Take a promotion schedule known at the forecast origin. The condition is whether promotion will be active; do not define it from the future sales outcome.
Set D=0 for inactive and D=1 for active. The two values encode the two permitted settings.
Check the displayed route: known schedule to indicator to a prediction input. The diagram is generated in code from those labels.
Keep a threshold, an indicator and a regime distinct: the cutoff defines a condition, the indicator encodes its truth, and the regime names the setting.
slide_steps: Read the promotion schedule available at the origin.
Encode inactive as 0 and active as 1.
Use that value without looking at the future outcome.
practice: Encode the schedule [inactive, active, active, inactive] as an array.

title: Calculate a promotion interaction
concept: An interaction lets the response to x depend on another input.
steps: Use the same constructed rule everywhere: predicted y = 10 + 2x + 5D + 3xD. The input x and promotion D must already be known.
Set x=2 and D=0. Both promotion terms vanish, leaving 10+4=14.
Set x=2 and D=1. Add the contributions 10, 4, 5 and 6 to obtain 25. Over the full x grid, the two rules are 10+2x and 15+5x.
Compare starting levels and slopes in the plotted lines. Switching D changes both in this example; it is not evidence of a causal promotion effect.
slide_steps: At x=2, set D=0: prediction 14.
At x=2, set D=1: prediction 25.
Compare starting levels 10/15 and slopes 2/5.
practice: At x=4, calculate D=0 and D=1; explain each contribution.

title: Read roots, branches, leaves and depth
concept: A regression tree routes a known input through questions to a stored numerical mean.
steps: Fit the eight traffic/sales pairs used in Example 4.5. The root contains eight observations and asks whether yesterday's traffic is at most 50.
Follow Yes or No to the two leaves. A split is the question; branches are its answers; leaves are the terminal prediction groups.
Fit a second tree with maximum depth two on the same pairs. Count splits along a case's path: root depth zero, first answer depth one, second answer depth two.
Read the plotted fitted structure rather than counting leaves as depth. In the depth-two tree, the four stored means are 22, 30, 62 and 70.
slide_steps: Start at the root: eight days, traffic cutoff 50.
Follow a branch to a leaf mean of 26 or 66.
Count split questions along the path to measure depth.
practice: Route traffic 20 through the depth-two tree and report its leaf prediction.

title: Compute leaf means and route new cases
concept: A squared-error regression leaf predicts its training outcome mean.
steps: Pair traffic [10,20,30,40,60,70,80,90] with sales [20,24,28,32,60,64,68,72]. The input precedes the sales target.
Split traffic at 50. Average the four left outcomes to get 26 and the four right outcomes to get 66.
Route the new input 35 to the left and 75 to the right. The computed predictions are 26 and 66; the unknown new outcomes are never used in routing.
Read the fitted graph as two constant regions, not a sloping interpolation within each leaf.
slide_steps: Split the same eight training pairs at traffic 50.
Average left sales to 26 and right sales to 66.
Route inputs 35/75 to predictions 26/66.
practice: Predict for traffic 50 and 51; explain the boundary convention.

title: Choose a split by its immediate training gain
concept: Greedy fitting chooses the best current training step, not an entire future tree.
steps: Keep the eight pairs fixed. Without splitting, the mean sales value is 46; squared distances from that mean sum to 3360.
At cutoff 50, the two within-leaf squared-error sums are 80 and 80, giving total 160.
Subtract 160 from 3360: the immediate training reduction is 3200. The candidate-cutoff table is computed for all seven separating cutoffs.
Find the minimum of the plotted candidate scores. This explains the fitted cutoff 50 but does not measure validation improvement.
slide_steps: One group: mean 46; training squared error 3360.
Cut at 50: two squared-error sums of 80.
Choose total 160, a training reduction of 3200.
practice: Calculate the training squared-error sum at cutoff 35 and compare it with 160.

title: Connect rectangles to a conditional tree
concept: One-input splits divide two-input space into rectangular prediction regions.
steps: Construct twelve cases from traffic [10,20,40,60,80,90] crossed with promotion D=0 or 1. This is a different labeled toy dataset from Example 4.3.
Assign sales 20 when traffic is at most 50. Above 50, assign 30 without promotion and 50 with promotion.
Fit the depth-two tree. It first separates traffic and then asks about promotion only inside the high-traffic branch.
Predict [35,0], [35,1], [75,0] and [75,1]. The outputs 20,20,30,50 connect the rectangular colors to the tree's conditional routes.
slide_steps: Build 12 traffic/promotion pairs with outcomes 20/30/50.
Split on traffic, then promotion within high traffic.
Check the four predictions: 20, 20, 30, 50.
practice: Why does changing D at traffic 35 leave the prediction unchanged? Verify in code.

title: Prepare the classroom demand example
concept: Simulation creates artificial observations from stated rules; these are not market data.
steps: Load the local business_demand.csv copied from the existing classroom package. It contains 180 simulated daily observations, source seed 417.
Create demand one day and two days earlier. Removing the first two unavailable lags leaves 178 usable rows.
Preserve date order. Use the first 124 rows for training, the next 27 for validation and the last 27 for final testing.
Read the date-series graph and the shaded periods. Both predictors are observed before the current demand target; no download fallback changes the data source.
slide_steps: Load the 180-day local classroom simulation.
Create two earlier-demand inputs; keep 178 usable rows.
Split by date into 124 / 27 / 27 cases.
practice: Print the first and last date of each block and verify their order.

title: Vary one tree control at a time
concept: Depth, leaf size and pruning constrain different aspects of a tree.
steps: In the left panel, vary maximum depth from one to eight with minimum leaf size held at two. Compute training and validation RMSE on fixed dates.
In the middle panel, vary minimum leaf size across 1,2,4,8,16 while maximum depth is eight.
In the right panel, vary pruning strength across 0,5,20,80,200, with minimum leaf size two. Count the remaining leaves.
These conditional comparisons explain the controls. They do not replace the joint depth/leaf-size search in Example 4.10.
slide_steps: Depth panel: hold minimum leaf size at 2.
Leaf-size panel: hold maximum depth at 8.
Pruning panel: count leaves as pruning strength increases.
practice: Fit depth=8 with minimum leaf sizes 1 and 16; compare leaf counts and validation errors.

title: Select depth and leaf size together
concept: A grid tries a list of candidate settings; here every depth/leaf-size pair is compared.
steps: Cross eight maximum depths with five minimum leaf sizes, producing forty candidate pairs.
Fit each candidate using the same 124 training rows and evaluate it on the same 27 validation rows.
Select the pair with the smallest validation RMSE. This run chooses depth five and leaf size four, with validation RMSE about 20.63.
Read the marked heatmap cell, then carry that pair to refitting. The final test is not used to select it.
slide_steps: Try 8 depths × 5 leaf sizes = 40 pairs.
Use the same training and validation rows for every pair.
Select depth 5, leaf size 4; validation RMSE 20.63.
practice: Restrict the grid to depths 2,3,5 and leaf sizes 4,8; select using validation only.

title: Change one leaf while fixing the query
concept: A model-sensitivity comparison keeps the prediction case fixed.
steps: Keep the right-leaf outcomes 60,64,68,72 and the traffic threshold 50. Their mean is 66.
Replace only the first outcome, 60, with 100. The right-leaf mean becomes 76.
Query the same input 75 before and after the replacement. The prediction rises by ten without changing the case.
This holds the split fixed to isolate the leaf average. It is not a claim that a newly optimized full tree must retain the same split.
slide_steps: Hold the split and input 75 fixed.
Replace outcome 60 with 100 in the same leaf.
Compare the means: 66 → 76.
practice: Replace 60 with 80 instead; predict the new mean before running the calculation.

title: Expand one model into a forest
concept: An ensemble combines fitted models; a random forest averages varied fitted trees.
steps: Identify one decision-tree diagram as one base learner, using the node and leaf meanings established in Example 4.4.
Expand it into a collection of seven schematic trees. Different structures represent possible fitted rules; seven is a drawing choice, not a required forest size.
Send the same known input case through all member rules rather than comparing different cases.
Combine the numerical predictions by their mean. The next examples show how rows and candidate inputs vary and how the average is computed.
slide_steps: One diagram represents one fitted tree.
Expand to a collection and route the same case through each.
Average numerical predictions from the member trees.
practice: Explain why showing seven trees does not define a required model hyperparameter.

title: Draw training rows with replacement
concept: With replacement means a selected row remains eligible to be drawn again.
steps: Start both draws from the same training pool A,B,C,D. The second tree does not draw from the first tree's bag.
The first constructed draw is A,A,C,D: A repeats and B is absent.
The second draw is A,B,B,D: B repeats and C is absent. Each bag still contains four selected rows.
The branching arrows show parallel resampling from the original pool. Every row must belong to the permitted training history.
slide_steps: Start each tree from the original pool A,B,C,D.
Draw A,A,C,D for one and A,B,B,D for another.
Identify repeated and missing rows in each bag.
practice: Use numpy to draw four identifiers with replacement; count repeats.

title: Inspect candidate feature draws
concept: Feature subsampling restricts the input columns that may compete at a split.
steps: Use four illustrative input names: Traffic, Advertising, Weather and Promotion.
With seed 417, draw two distinct candidate columns at each of three illustrative nodes. The generated pairs are Promotion/Traffic, Advertising/Promotion and Promotion/Advertising.
The third pair repeats the second set in a different order. Random draws may repeat a subset; different draws need not produce different sets.
A fixed seed reproduces these choices. It does not test sensitivity to a different training sample.
slide_steps: Start with four named input columns.
Draw two candidates per node with seed 417.
A subset may repeat; a seed makes the draws reproducible.
practice: Change the seed to 418 and print the three new candidate sets.

title: Fit three trees and average one shared query
concept: A regression forest averages numerical member predictions for the same case.
steps: Use a six-row constructed pool: identifiers L,A,B,C,D,E; inputs [-1,1,1,1,1,1]; outcomes [10,40,50,60,70,80].
Fit three depth-one trees to bags [L,A,A,B,C,C], [L,A,B,C,D,E] and [L,C,C,D,E,E]. Each learned root splits x at zero.
Query x=1. The right-leaf outcome means are 50,60,70. These are predictions of the actual fitted trees, not numbers attached to unrelated tree pictures.
Add 50+60+70 and divide by three to get 60. The left query x=-1 would return 10 from every tree.
slide_steps: Fit three stated bootstrap bags from the same six-row pool.
At x=1, read the fitted leaf means 50, 60, 70.
Average the three predictions to obtain 60.
practice: Query x=-1 for all three trees and calculate their average.

title: Compare offsetting and shared errors
concept: Averaging can offset differing errors but cannot remove an identical shared error.
steps: Hold the target case fixed. Construct three errors +6,-3,-3, expressed as prediction minus target.
Calculate their mean: zero. The plotted average marker falls on the zero-error reference.
Now change the error vector to +6,+6,+6. Its mean remains +6; the average marker stays on the same side as every member.
These are controlled illustrations of cancellation and shared error, not a proof that a forest achieves a given accuracy.
slide_steps: Use one fixed target and errors +6, -3, -3.
Their mean is 0: the misses offset.
Repeat with +6,+6,+6; the mean remains +6.
practice: Calculate the average error for [6,-3,0] and for [4,4,4].

title: Keep the forest inside chronological training
concept: Random tree construction does not authorize future rows in the training history.
steps: Reuse the chronological blocks from Example 4.8: 124 training, 27 validation and 27 test rows.
Permit internal bootstrap draws only from the current training block. Feature-subset settings concern columns, not permission to move future dates into training.
Use validation to choose development settings and retain the final test for the settled procedure.
Distinguish the learner's row resampling from the block-bootstrap uncertainty calculation introduced in Lecture 2.
slide_steps: Fit and resample within the 124-row training history.
Use the next 27 rows for model development.
Keep the final 27 rows for settled procedures.
practice: Generate training bootstrap identifiers and verify that their dates never exceed the training end.

title: Normalize three split-credit totals
concept: Normalizing divides each credit by a positive total so the shares sum to one.
steps: Use the constructed raw credits 60,30,10 for three illustrative inputs. This hand calculation is separate from the two-input classroom forest.
Add the credits: the total is 100.
Divide each credit by 100 to obtain 0.60,0.30,0.10, and check that the shares sum to one.
Read these as shares of the chosen training split score, not percentages of future accuracy.
slide_steps: Add constructed credits 60 + 30 + 10 = 100.
Divide each credit by 100: 0.60, 0.30, 0.10.
Interpret shares of split credits, not future accuracy.
practice: Normalize [6,3,1] and compare its shares with [60,30,10].

title: Read the fitted forest importance
concept: Feature importance measures a fitted model's use of an input under a specified scoring procedure.
steps: Fit the classroom forest on the 124 training rows with 100 trees, depth five, minimum leaf size eight, one candidate input per split and seed 417.
Read the fitted training split-credit shares for the two lagged-demand inputs. They are approximately 0.699 and 0.301.
Check the total of the positive normalized shares. The two-input score is not the separate three-input normalization example.
Keep training split importance distinct from permutation importance: one credits training splits; the other changes input alignment and reevaluates a fixed model.

As a separate edge case, fit a forest with minimum split size 200 to only 124 training rows. It cannot form effective splits, and both importance entries are zero. This is not a set of normalized positive credits.
slide_steps: Read the fitted two-input classroom forest.
Its split-credit shares are approximately 0.699 and 0.301.
Keep this training score distinct from a shuffle diagnostic.
practice: Print the fitted importance sum and explain why it is not a causal effect.

title: Shuffle one validation input at a time
concept: Permutation importance reevaluates a fixed model after an input is rearranged.
steps: Keep the trained classroom forest and all 27 validation outcomes fixed. Its unshuffled validation RMSE is about 23.33.
Rearrange one input column, leaving its values intact but changing their row alignment. The left panel displays a five-row illustration, not all evaluation rows.
Repeat twenty rearrangements per input over the full validation block. Mean RMSE is approximately 32.72 for the one-day lag shuffle and 26.27 for the two-day lag shuffle.
Compare those errors with the same unshuffled value. The increases are approximately 9.39 and 2.93 demand units; these are development diagnostics.
slide_steps: Keep model, outcomes and 27 validation dates fixed.
Shuffle one column twenty times.
Compare RMSE 23.33 with means 32.72 and 26.27.
practice: Repeat with five shuffles and compare the mean and spread with the twenty-shuffle calculation.

title: Trace substitute information through two columns
concept: Related predictors can supply substitute information to a fitted model.
steps: Construct twenty counter values and copy the same values into a second column. The two traces deliberately overlap.
Rearranging one column leaves the other column's values and ordering intact.
Identify exactly which information connection the perturbation breaks and which substitute remains.
The plot illustrates the information structure. It is not itself a measured claim about a trained model's permutation score; any such score must be computed and labeled separately.
slide_steps: Create two identical constructed counter traces.
Rearrange one; the second trace remains intact.
Distinguish the diagram from a measured importance score.
practice: Fit a model using the duplicate columns; compare shuffling one column with shuffling both.

title: Preserve a pipeline and compare reporting units
concept: A pipeline applies ordered preparation and model steps; changing units can preserve tree groups.
steps: Fit any learned preparation and the prediction rule using permitted earlier observations. Apply the stored procedure to later inputs.
Reuse the eight traffic/sales pairs. Fit once with traffic in customers, and once with traffic divided by 100, reported in hundreds of customers.
The learned cutoffs are 50 customers and approximately 0.5 hundreds. Queries 35 and 75 become 0.35 and 0.75.
Both fitted trees give predictions 26 and 66. Floating-point cutoff display can differ slightly, but the fitted group assignments and predictions agree for these cases.
slide_steps: Fit the same eight pairs in customers and hundreds.
Compare cutoffs 50 and approximately 0.5.
Queries 35/75 and 0.35/0.75 both predict 26/66.
practice: Rescale traffic by 10 instead and verify the same predictions.

title: Report validation and refitted test results
concept: Model comparison uses the same target, dates and units, with settings chosen before final testing.
steps: Compare Linear, Quadratic, Ridge, the jointly selected Tree, the preset Forest and Persistence on the same validation dates.
The validation RMSE values are approximately 20.62, 21.09, 20.62, 20.63, 23.33, 22.89. Linear, ridge and tree are very close; a forest win is not assumed.
Refit each settled learned procedure using training plus validation. Then predict the final 27 dates; persistence uses the latest observed demand directly.
Report the test scores without retuning: approximately 28.77, 29.11, 28.77, 30.90, 32.55, 29.12 in the same model order. These results concern this simulation, not a universal ranking.
slide_steps: Compare all candidates on identical validation dates.
Refit settled procedures on training plus validation.
Report test results without selecting from the test.
practice: Export the table and identify a comparison that is nearly tied on validation but differs on test.

title: Refit while holding reference inputs fixed
concept: Changing the training sample and changing the prediction case answer different questions.
steps: Construct low-lag and high-lag reference input pairs from the training-data range. Keep both vectors unchanged throughout the diagnostic.
Fit the same selected tree and preset forest on six 80-day windows ending at rows 80,90,100,110,120,124 within training history.
After each fit, predict the two unchanged vectors and plot each vector in its own panel.
Variation along a panel tracks refit sensitivity for a fixed case. A difference between panels reflects different input conditions and must not be called model instability.
slide_steps: Choose two fixed reference input vectors.
Refit six 80-day windows inside training history.
Compare predictions within each unchanged-case panel.
practice: Print the two reference vectors and the prediction spread across refits for each model and case.

title: Predict beyond the observed input range
concept: Extrapolation applies a rule outside represented input conditions.
steps: Reuse the same eight traffic/sales training pairs, whose largest observed input is 90.
Fit the one-split tree and linear regression using only those pairs.
Query inputs out to 140. The tree keeps returning its right-leaf mean 66; the fitted linear rule continues its line.
Read the shaded region as outside the training input range. No target outcomes in that region were supplied to validate either continuation.
slide_steps: Fit the same eight pairs, with largest input 90.
Extend queries to 140 without adding outcomes.
The tree stays at leaf mean 66 outside its range.
practice: Compare both predictions at traffic 120; explain what remains unknown about their accuracy.
